To: All staff, Customer Service
From: Head of Operations
Date: 12 March
Subject: Changes to the returns procedure from 1 April

From next month, returns will no longer be accepted at the counter on the ground floor. Customers sending items back must use the prepaid label enclosed with their original order, and post the parcel from any collection point.

Training on the new procedure will run on 25 and 26 March, and attendance is required for anyone who deals with customers directly.

points: BEC 口语 Part 3 是「一分钟准备 + 一分钟发言」，评分看结构和互动，不看观点对错

Let me start with the benefits. The clearest one for us is retention. Two of the people we lost last year said in their exit interviews that the commute was the deciding factor, and both were doing work that does not require them to be in the building.

However, there are real difficulties. Our work is not evenly suited to remote arrangements. A designer who needs to sit with a client cannot do that from home, and if the same policy applies to everyone, the people who can work remotely will take the benefit while the others feel penalised. There is also the question of how we hand work over between teams.

On balance, I would recommend allowing it, but not as a general entitlement. I would suggest a trial for six months, limited to roles where the work is measurable on its own, with one fixed day a week when everyone is in the office. That keeps the handover working and gives us evidence before we make it permanent.

items.script:
W: Professor Hale, you have spent ten years studying how cities cope with extreme heat. What surprised you most?
M: I expected the problem to be about temperature. It turned out to be about time. A neighbourhood that gets shade for six hours a day and one that gets it for two are both described as hot, but the people living in them have very different days.

items.title: Repair Cafés and the Cost of Throwing Things Away
passage:
The first repair café opened in Amsterdam in 2009, in a small hall with a few tables and a handful of volunteers who knew how to handle a soldering iron. The idea was simple: people would bring broken goods, and someone would help them fix the goods on the spot. Fifteen years later there are more than two thousand such gatherings worldwide, and the model has barely changed. What has changed is the reason people give for coming.

In the early years, visitors talked about money. A toaster that could be repaired for nothing was obviously better than a new one that cost thirty euros. Today, volunteers report that the most common opening line is not about price at all. It is about waste. People have begun to see the objects in their kitchens and cupboards as things they are responsible for, rather than as disposable packaging around a useful few months. That shift matters, because it is the one thing a recycling bin cannot produce. Once an object is in the bin, its fate is out of your hands; while it is on the table, it is still yours to decide.

The volunteers are careful not to overstate what they achieve. A repair café cannot compete with a factory. Yet its founder argues that the numbers were never the point. The point, she says, is that a person who has watched a stranger open a machine and name the broken part will never again look at a similar object as a sealed box. That changed way of seeing, she believes, is worth more than the tonnes of waste the movement diverts each year.

questions.explain: In the early years, visitors talked about money.

options: It reduces the amount of broken equipment that is produced.
It gives people a sense of responsibility that recycling cannot create.

It makes volunteers more willing to give up their free time.

They argue that repair cafés could replace factories.
They insist that the weight of waste saved proves the point.
They admit that the movement has had almost no effect.
questions.explain: The volunteers are careful not to overstate what they achieve… the numbers were never the point —— 他们不夸大修好的数量。

items.title: Sleep, Memory and the Modern Schedule

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, sleep was treated as an interruption. The useful hours were the waking ones, and anyone who slept longer than necessary was assumed to be lazy. Only in the past twenty years has the opposite view become common: that sleep is not the absence of activity but one of the most demanding things the brain does.

The evidence for this came first from memory experiments. Volunteers who learned a list of word pairs and then slept for eight hours recalled far more of them the next morning than volunteers who stayed awake the same length of time. Crucially, the sleeping group had spent no extra time studying. The improvement had happened while they were, by every outward measure, doing nothing at all.

Imaging studies explained how. During deep sleep the brain replays the day's patterns at high speed, and the hippocampus, a structure that holds new information only briefly, passes it to the cortex for long-term storage. Cut the sleep short and the transfer is incomplete. The material is not erased; it becomes harder to reach, which is why a student can recognise an answer without being able to produce it.

What followed was less scientific and more commercial. An industry grew up around the finding, selling mattresses, trackers and supplements, much of it with weak evidence behind it. Researchers themselves were uncomfortable with this. Their message had been that sleep is ordinary, universal and free. It was turned into a product to be optimised, and the anxiety that came with the product may itself keep people awake.

Schools and employers have been slower to move, because the costs of short sleep fall on individuals while the benefits of long hours are easy to see on a spreadsheet. A few districts have shifted the start of the school day later for teenagers, whose body clocks run late by biology rather than choice. The measured results have been modest but consistent, with better attendance and fewer road accidents among young drivers in the morning.

The most stubborn obstacle is cultural. Sleeping well is still, in many workplaces, treated as a sign that someone is not committed. Until that changes, individuals will keep trading sleep for the appearance of effort, and the loss will be counted somewhere else, in mistakes, in illness, or in years.

statements.s: Experiments showed that people who slept retained more than people who stayed awake for the same period without further study.
The shift of information from short-term to long-term storage is completed during deep sleep.
Commercial products based on sleep research were often supported by little evidence.
Teenagers naturally tend to fall asleep and wake later than adults.
In many workplaces, sleeping well is still read as a lack of dedication.

items.sample:
Learning to use digital tools is no longer an extra skill that sits beside your main subject. For most students it is part of the subject itself.

The obvious benefit is speed. A question that once meant a walk to the library is now answered in seconds. The risk is that speed feels like accuracy. The first result on a search page is chosen by a machine that is optimising for attention, not for truth, and it can be confidently wrong. A student who cannot tell the difference will work quickly and learn little.

So the habit worth building early is simple: whenever a claim matters, look for a second source that was written independently. If two sources disagree, that disagreement is information too.

My advice to a new student would be this. Use the tools, and treat every single one of them as a starting point rather than an answer.

items.title: 汉译英：二十四节气
items.material: 二十四节气是中国古人根据太阳周年运动总结出来的一套时间知识体系。它把一年分成二十四段，每一段都对应着气候的变化和农事的节奏。在没有天气预报的年代，农民靠它决定什么时候播种、什么时候收割。今天，虽然大多数人已经不再种地，但节气仍然留在日常生活里：清明节要去扫墓，冬至许多家庭会一起吃饺子。2016 年，二十四节气被列入联合国教科文组织人类非物质文化遗产代表作名录。
points: 「二十四节气」译成 the 24 solar terms（这是通用译法）
「时间知识体系」可以译成 a system of knowledge about time
「对应着」用 correspond to 比 match 更准确
「靠它决定」用 depend on it to decide / use it to decide
「被列入……名录」用 was added to the list / was inscribed on the list，注意要用被动
最后一句主语是「二十四节气」，别把主语换成 UNESCO
items.reference: The 24 solar terms are a system of knowledge about time that the ancient Chinese developed from the annual movement of the sun. It divides a year into twenty-four parts, each corresponding to a change in the weather and to the rhythm of farm work. In an age without weather forecasts, farmers depended on it to decide when to sow and when to harvest. Today, although most people no longer work on the land, the solar terms are still part of daily life: people visit family graves during Qingming, and many families eat dumplings together at the winter solstice. In 2016, the 24 solar terms were added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The suggestion that universities should teach practical skills rather than theory rests on a reasonable observation: many graduates leave with knowledge they cannot apply. However, I disagree with the proposal as it stands, because the distinction it relies on is weaker than it appears.

The first reason is that most practical skills cannot be taught in the abstract. A student who learns to read a balance sheet without understanding why the numbers behave as they do can follow a procedure but cannot judge whether the result is plausible. The theory is what allows the procedure to be used in an unfamiliar case, and the unfamiliar case is exactly what employment consists of.

The second reason is that the labour market changes faster than curricula. A university that trains students for today's tools produces graduates whose skills expire within a decade. What remains valuable is the ability to learn a new tool, which depends on understanding principles rather than procedures.

I therefore agree that universities should pay more attention to application, but not at the cost of theory. The two are not rivals. A course that teaches a method without its explanation is not more practical; it is simply shorter. The strongest programmes combine them deliberately, and that is what universities should be asked to do.

points: GRE Issue 评分看「论证的复杂度」，不是看立场 —— 一边倒的答案通常拿不到高分

The statement is attractive because the historical cases that support it are memorable: a single person who asks a question that everyone else has accepted can redirect an entire field. But the examples that support it are selected, and the claim as written is too strong to be correct in general.

Consider what questioning authority actually requires. It requires the questioner to have enough standing to be heard, and enough knowledge to judge when the authority is wrong. Neither is distributed evenly. In a society where most people lack the relevant expertise, universal scepticism does not produce better decisions; it produces a market in confident voices, since a claim that is easy to understand will travel further than one that is correct. The failure mode of uncritical deference is that bad ideas persist. The failure mode of indiscriminate scepticism is that they are replaced by worse ones.

The condition under which the statement holds is narrower but still important. Questioning is valuable where the cost of being wrong is high, where evidence can be produced, and where the questioner has some way to evaluate the answer. Those conditions describe science, medicine and, increasingly, the management of public data. They do not describe every decision a society makes.

So the statement should be revised rather than accepted. What a society needs is not a general willingness to question authority, but reliable institutions that make questioning useful — places where a doubt can be tested rather than merely broadcast.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, sleeping trains were how Europe travelled. Then cheap flights arrived, and one route after another was closed. By 2015 only a handful remained, and industry analysts had written the whole category off as a museum piece.

The revival that followed surprised almost everyone. It began with a shift in how a certain kind of traveller counted cost. A flight may be cheaper than a berth, but it also requires a night in a hotel at one end or the other, and it consumes a working day. Once those are added, the arithmetic changes, and for a business traveller the train becomes competitive. Environmental concern played a part, but interviews with passengers suggest it was rarely the main reason for choosing the train. Comfort, and the fact that the journey replaces accommodation rather than adding to it, came up far more often.

passage: Peer review is usually described as the process by which experts decide whether a piece of research deserves publication. In practice it is better understood as a form of unpaid labour that has been asked to do three jobs at once: to check whether the work is sound, to judge whether it is important, and to defend the journal against the accusation that it publishes anything. These three aims pull in different directions, and the system has never been given the time or the money to satisfy all of them.

The strain shows up in the reviews themselves. A study of referee reports in one large field found that the median report ran to fewer than four hundred words, and that reviewers spent, on average, about half a day on each paper. Four hundred words is a short essay written by an expert who has not been paid, who is reading outside working hours, and who knows that the authors may be better informed than he is. Under those conditions, reviewers do what anyone would do: they look for the things that are quickest to check and hardest to argue with. Formatting, statistics and obviously missing citations get caught. A clever study that asks the wrong question is much more likely to pass.

None of this means peer review is worthless. Alternatives that have been tried — publishing everything and letting readers judge, or replacing reviewers with metrics — have performed worse on almost every measure. The point is narrower and more uncomfortable: the system is being praised for a property it cannot reliably deliver. It filters out work that looks careless. It does not, and cannot, tell you which papers will still be read in twenty years.

We have maps, we have satellites, and we thought we would simply measure what was already there. It turned out that satellites cannot see a tree that stands under a larger tree, and they cannot see one that grows in a courtyard. passage: Anyone who has run a small organisation knows an odd fact about correspondence: a letter takes far longer to answer than an email, and yet it is the letter that gets answered first. The explanation usually offered is respect — that a letter cost the sender money and time, and that this deserves a reply. The explanation is incomplete. The real reason is that a letter arrives with a shape.

An email can be read in four seconds and answered in twenty, or left for a month, and nothing about it says which is appropriate. Its cost of delay is invisible. A letter announces its own importance: the paper, the signature, the fact that somebody had to find an envelope. Because the sender has visibly spent something, the receiver can estimate what a failure to reply would mean. That estimate is what produces the quick response — not politeness, but information.

This has an uncomfortable application to the modern office. When an organisation moves all of its communication to a channel where nothing carries a cost, it does not merely lose letters. It loses the signal that used to tell people which messages mattered. Every message then looks equally cheap, so every message is treated as equally optional, and the ones that genuinely matter are delayed along with the ones that do not. Managers notice the delay and respond by asking for quicker replies, which adds a signal that costs nothing and is therefore ignored.

Before 1956, moving goods across an ocean was a job for people rather than machines. A ship might spend as long in port as it did at sea, because every crate had to be lifted out of a lorry, set down on the dock, counted, and lifted again into the hold. The cost of loading was often greater than the cost of the voyage, and the men who did the loading were organised, well paid and, in most ports, able to control the pace of the work. Goods were handled so many times that theft and breakage were ordinary expenses, budgeted for like fuel.

The change came from a lorry owner rather than a shipowner. Malcom McLean had built a haulage business in North Carolina and had grown tired of watching his vehicles wait at the dockside. His idea was not new — boxes had been used on railways for decades — but he saw that the box had to be standard. If every company used a different size, each would still need its own cranes, and the saving would vanish. He settled on a length that could be carried by a lorry, a railway wagon and a ship, and he was willing to buy both the ships and the ports to prove it worked.

The resistance he met was not technical. Dockworkers understood immediately that a system which moved boxes with cranes would need far fewer of them, and they struck, in some ports for months. Their objection was reasonable, and their prediction was correct: employment in the docks fell sharply over the following twenty years. What is less often noticed is what happened elsewhere. Because shipping became cheap, it became practical to manufacture in one country and sell in another, and the work that left the docks reappeared inland, in warehouses and factories, in numbers that no one in 1956 had forecast.

The economic effect was not confined to transport. When the cost of moving a finished good across an ocean falls to a small fraction of its price, the location of production stops being decided by distance from the customer and starts being decided by the cost of labour and land. Ports that had been wealthy for centuries because they were convenient lost their advantage, and cities that had been irrelevant acquired it. The losers and the winners were not the ones the industry had expected.

questions.q: According to the first paragraph, why did ships spend as long in port as at sea before 1956?
options: Ports lacked the cranes needed to lift heavy loads.
Every crate had to be handled several times by hand.
Ships were not designed to cross oceans quickly.
Customs inspections were carried out on board.
questions.explain: every crate had to be lifted out of a lorry, set down on the dock, counted, and lifted again into the hold

questions.q: What does the passage say about theft and breakage before 1956?
options: They were rare enough to be ignored.
They were treated as a normal, budgeted cost.
They were the main reason dockworkers were well paid.
They occurred mainly during the sea voyage.
questions.explain: theft and breakage were ordinary expenses, budgeted for like fuel

questions.q: Why did McLean insist that the container be a standard size?
options: A standard size was cheaper to manufacture.
Railways refused to carry boxes of other sizes.
If each company used its own size, each would need its own equipment and the saving would be lost.
Governments required a single size for safety reasons.
questions.explain: If every company used a different size, each would still need its own cranes, and the saving would vanish.

questions.q: What was the nature of the opposition McLean faced?
options: Engineers doubted that cranes could lift loaded containers.
Shipowners believed the system would be too costly.
Dockworkers feared, correctly, that far fewer of them would be needed.
Governments objected to the loss of customs revenue.
questions.explain: Dockworkers understood immediately that a system which moved boxes with cranes would need far fewer of them… and their prediction was correct

questions.q: According to the final paragraph, what determined where production was located once shipping became cheap?
options: The cost of labour and land.
The size of the domestic market.
questions.explain: starts being decided by the cost of labour and land

items.title: 听力：讲座（生物学 · 动物的「文化」）
items.script:
Professor: I want to spend today on a word that makes biologists uncomfortable, and that word is culture. When we say a behaviour is cultural, we usually mean it is learned from others rather than inherited, and that it varies between groups that are otherwise identical. For a long time the standard reply was that only humans do this. That reply is now very hard to defend.

Take the whales off the coast of New England. In the 1980s, one animal began feeding in a way nobody had recorded before: it would slap the surface with its tail, driving fish into a tight ball, and then feed on the ball. Within about ten years, most of the population was doing it. The behaviour did not spread along family lines — it spread between animals that spent time together. That is the pattern you would expect if it were being learned socially.

Now, you might object that copying a feeding trick is not culture. Fair enough. So here is a harder case. Different groups of the same species use different sounds, and the differences do not match the genetic differences between the groups. Two populations that are genetically almost identical can have almost completely different call repertoires. If the calls were inherited, that should not happen.

I should add one caution. Learning by imitation is expensive. It takes time, it can go wrong, and it exposes you to the errors of whoever you are copying. So we should expect animals to rely on it only where the environment is stable enough that what worked for someone else is likely to work for you.

questions.q: What is the professor's main purpose in giving this lecture?
options: To argue that culture is a useful concept in biology.
To explain why whale populations are declining.
To compare two species of whale.
To show that genetic inheritance explains all animal behaviour.
questions.explain: 全篇在为「动物也有文化（社会学习）」这个说法辩护，并给出两个证据。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention the feeding behaviour of whales in New England?
options: It shows that whales can be trained by researchers.
It spread between animals that spent time together rather than along family lines.
It is the oldest recorded example of tool use in the ocean.
It demonstrates that whales have a larger diet than was thought.
questions.explain: The behaviour did not spread along family lines — it spread between animals that spent time together.

questions.q: Why does the professor describe the difference in calls between populations as "a harder case"?
options: Because the calls are difficult for researchers to record.
Because the differences do not match the genetic differences between the groups.
Because only males produce the calls.
Because the calls change every year.
questions.explain: the differences do not match the genetic differences between the groups —— 若是遗传就不该如此。

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude towards learning by imitation?
options: It is always more efficient than learning alone.
It should be expected mainly in stable environments because it carries costs.
It is rare among animals other than humans.
It cannot be studied in the wild.
questions.explain: we should expect animals to rely on it only where the environment is stable enough…

items.title: 学术讨论写作（类似新托福 Writing for an Academic Discussion）
items.material:
Your professor is teaching a class on public policy. Write a post of about 150–200 words responding to the following question.

Professor: Many cities now publish detailed data about their own performance — how quickly potholes are fixed, how many buses arrive on time. Some argue this makes government more accountable. Others say that when people know they are being measured, they focus on the measure rather than the goal. What is your view?

Student A: I think publishing data is almost always good. If people can see the numbers, they can complain with evidence instead of opinion.

Student B: I disagree. My mother works for a city department, and she says the first thing that happened was that everyone stopped taking on difficult cases, because difficult cases make the numbers look bad.
points: 必须回应教授的问题，并且要明确提到至少一位同学的观点（这是这类题的要求）
不要只复述 A / B 的话，要表明你同意谁、或者对两者都提出修正
最好的落点是「指标会改变行为」这一层：指标有用，但不能拿它当目标本身
150–200 词；学术讨论写作不需要开头结尾的套话，直接给观点
items.sample:
Student B's point is the more important one, and I would push it further. Student A is right that data gives citizens something concrete to argue about, and that is a real gain. But B's mother is describing something that happens almost every time a measure becomes public, and it is not a sign of laziness.

When a number is attached to a person's performance, that number stops describing the work and starts shaping it. The mother's colleagues did not decide to be worse at their jobs. They responded rationally to a rule that made difficult cases expensive. Any department that measures only speed will get speed, and it will get it partly by declining the slow jobs.

The solution is not to stop publishing. It is to publish several numbers at once, including one that makes the difficult cases visible, so that avoiding them looks bad rather than clever.

items.title: 独立口语：15 秒准备，45 秒作答
items.material: Some students prefer to study in the morning; others prefer to study late at night. Which do you prefer, and why? Give specific reasons and details in your answer.
points: 准备 15 秒、作答 45 秒 —— 时间极短，必须一开始就给出选择，不要拖
结构：一句话表态 → 两个理由 → 各配一个具体细节（具体到时间、地点、发生过什么事）
托福口语评分看的是「能不能把理由说清楚」，不是观点多深刻 —— 别追求复杂观点
不要背模板句。背模板会占掉宝贵的几秒，而且听起来像在念
45 秒大约 90–110 词，语速正常即可，不要为了多说而赶
items.sample:
I prefer studying early in the morning, mainly because of how my attention works before anyone else is awake.

Last semester I tried studying at night for about three weeks. The problem was not that I was tired. It was that every message and every notification arrived while I was reading, so I was restarting the same paragraph over and over.

In the morning there is nothing to interrupt me. I get up at six, and from six to eight the flat is completely quiet. In those two hours I can finish what used to take me an entire evening. That is the whole reason — it is not discipline, it is just that nobody is awake to distract me.
